title: Cobbleway Parcels: why is the hub falling behind?
prompt: Cobbleway Parcels is a UK parcel carrier. Its main sorting hub in the Midlands has fallen behind: on most nights it cannot sort every parcel in time for the morning delivery vans, so tens of thousands of parcels arrive a day late. The operations director wants to spend £15 million on a second sorting machine. The CEO has asked you to work out what is going wrong and whether the new machine is the right fix. How would you approach this?

facts.answer: Lorries arrive from 7pm to midnight and wait in the yard until a dock door is free. The hub sorts from 8pm to 4am, eight hours. All four steps run at the same time as one flow, and vans leave from 5am.
The hub now handles about 240,000 parcels a night, up from about 200,000 two years ago. Volume is growing about 10% a year and is expected to keep doing so.

There are four steps: unloading lorries at the docks; induction, where staff place each parcel label-up on the sorting machine's belts; the automated sorting machine, which reads each label and sends the parcel to the chute for its delivery route; and loading the route cages onto vans.

On a typical night tens of thousands of parcels miss the 4am cut-off. A small day shift sorts them and they go out a day late. Complaints have tripled this year. Two large online retailers, which together send about 15% of the hub's parcels, have warned they may move to another carrier unless deliveries are back on time within three months.

facts.question_topic: Why the operations director wants a machine
facts.answer: Every night parcels pile up beside the sorting machine, waiting to be placed on it, so he believes the machine is too slow.
The hub has 50 induction stations, each needing one person. Most induction staff are agency workers, and on a typical night about 10 stations are empty because workers do not turn up.
Small soft parcels in plastic bags, mostly from online clothing sellers, have grown as a share of volume. They slide on the belts and take longer to place label-up than boxes.

The current machine is reliable, with less than 2% downtime. A second machine would cost £15m and take 18 months to install. The building has space for it. It would be fed from the same 50 induction stations; it would not add any.

A permanent night worker costs about £33,000 a year. Hiring 12, enough to fill 8 more induction stations every night after holidays and sickness, would cost about £0.4m a year; filling all 10 empty stations would take about 15 people. Recruiting and training takes about six weeks.
Other hubs are not part of this case. The CEO would prefer not to spend £15m unless it is clearly needed.

math.question: How many parcels an hour must the hub handle to sort every parcel by 4am?
math.working: 240,000 parcels over 8 hours (8pm to 4am) is 30,000 parcels an hour.

math.question: With induction as the slowest step, how many parcels a night miss the 4am cut-off?
math.working: Induction handles 25,000 an hour x 8 hours = 200,000 parcels. 240,000 - 200,000 = 40,000 parcels miss the cut-off, about one in six.

math.question: At today's speed per person, how many induction stations must be staffed to keep up with tonight's volume?
math.working: 30,000 parcels an hour / 625 per person = 48 stations. The hub has 50, so it needs 8 more staffed than the 40 it has on a typical night, with almost no slack.

math.question: If volume grows 10% next year, how many parcels an hour will the hub need to handle?
math.working: 240,000 x 1.1 = 264,000 parcels a night. 264,000 / 8 = 33,000 an hour. That is above loading's 32,000, so loading becomes the next bottleneck. The sorting machine (40,000) still has room.

math.question: Next year, even with all 50 induction stations staffed, how many parcels must each person place per hour for induction to keep up?
math.working: Next year the hub needs 33,000 parcels an hour. 33,000 / 50 stations = 660 parcels per person per hour, up from 625 today. All 50 stations at today's speed give only 31,250 an hour (50 x 625), so filling stations is not enough: each person must also get faster, for example by taking soft parcels off the main belts.

brainstorm.question: What could Cobbleway do to raise induction output quickly, and what should it plan for next?
idea_bank: Replace unreliable agency workers with permanent night staff, or pay a bonus for turning up
Keep a pool of trained standby staff to fill empty stations each night
Hold the agency to a guaranteed fill rate, or add a second agency
Move staff from unloading, which has spare capacity, to induction during the busiest hours
Send small soft parcels to trays or a separate hand-sort line so they do not slow the main belts
Ask large senders to use boxes or pre-sort their parcels, with a discount for machine-friendly packaging
Redesign stations so parcels reach each person at the right height and pace
Ask some lorries to arrive earlier so sorting can start before 8pm
Add automatic induction equipment for standard boxes later on
Add van loading capacity before next year's growth
Draw up a capacity plan for every step: unloading runs out in about two years and the machine in about three
Track output per hour at every step each night to see where the bottleneck moves

must_mention: Induction is the bottleneck: 25,000 parcels an hour against 30,000 needed, so about 40,000 parcels a night miss the cut-off

model_answer_outline: Clarify: 240,000 parcels a night must be sorted between 8pm and 4am; volume grows 10% a year; tens of thousands of parcels a night are late, and two retailers with about 15% of volume want a fix within three months; the proposed fix is a £15m second machine that takes 18 months to install.
Structure: required rate, capacity of each step, the bottleneck and why it is slow, options with cost and time, future growth.

Analysis: the hub needs 30,000 parcels an hour. Unloading (36,000), the machine (40,000) and loading (32,000) can cope; induction (25,000) cannot, so output is 200,000 a night and 40,000 (one in six) are late. The pile of parcels beside the machine is the queue for induction, not a sign that the machine is slow.
Root cause: induction fell from 33,600 to 25,000 an hour because only 40 of 50 stations are staffed and soft parcels (now 40% of volume) slow each person from 700 to 625 an hour.

Maths: 48 staffed stations are needed at today's speed. Next year the hub needs 33,000 an hour: even all 50 stations at 625 give only 31,250, so each person must place about 660 an hour (back towards the 700 of two years ago), and loading (32,000) must grow too.

Recommendation: do not buy the second machine now. Hire permanent night staff (12 to 15 people, about £0.4m to £0.5m a year) so that 48 to 50 stations are filled every night, using standby agency staff and overtime for the six weeks this takes; set up a separate line for soft parcels to lift speed per person; and add loading capacity before next year. Risks: permanent staff may also miss shifts, and the retailers may leave before the fixes land, so report on-time delivery to them weekly. The machine reaches its limit in about three years and takes 18 months to install, so decide on it in about 18 months, as part of a plan for every step (unloading runs out in about two years).
